utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. The Defence simply wishes to inform the Chamber that we have our expert, Janko Vilicic, as part of our Defence team, while the examination of Mr. Berko Zecevic is in progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Welcome in the courtroom. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think perhaps it would be more convenient if we proceed, and this is really in the hands in the Court, with the exhibits of the witness from yesterday. There was a holdover --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is the first thing we should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But before we proceed to that, I wonder if my learned friend could spell the surname of the expert. I have the pronunciation, but the spelling I think I'm not too sure of. If she may, I would be obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, would you spell the surname of the expert who is assisting you today.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Janko Vilicic, Dr., Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Vilicic is written V-i-l-i-c-i-c?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] V-i-l-c-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Vilcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please guide us the through the documents that were tendered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document, Your Honour, is Defence Exhibit 137, letter to commander of UNPROFOR, number 09/20-94. D138, letter from the head of the state of the army of Republika Srpska, dated 5/2/1994, number 10-24-28. And D139, letter from Radovan Karadzic dated 26 July, 1994, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to make things perfectly clear, the name of the witness is Vilivic. An "i" is missing after the "l," between the "l" and the "c." If you want me to spell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We took note of that now. We have V-i-l-i-c-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the documents are admitted into evidence, that is D137, D138 and 139.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I be excused, Mr. President? Mr. Stamp is taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before Mr. Stamp is authorised to bring in the next witness, I would like to say something and consult with you, that is to say the fashion in which the consequences of your new jurisprudence should apply to the transcript. If you understand -- if you remember yesterday, we spoke of the possibility of speaking of transcript problems at the end of the session. Yesterday, we were not able to do that. I am not blaming anyone, but the Prosecution needed more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since we had no time yesterday to do it, if there is any problem with the transcript which could not be solved by bringing it to the attention of the Registry at a later stage, please do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There were two problems, but I didn't have the time to verify them, and this is another issue that I have to bring up. These are pages 1113, where the name -- where "civil" was not introduced in the French text. The other is 229, where all the specifications of crater analysis were not sufficiently or correctly translated into French. And I think there are some minor issues which I do not want to deal with now. What I wish to say is that while the Defence is trying to gain time for the Prosecution, I don't think it is admissible that we ask to spell out names that are very well-known like "Timisoara." That is like asking us to spell Gorazde or Sarajevo. I don't think that has any particular sense. And I think the Prosecution should bear this in mind, and I thank them in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both parties should keep in mind that they should assist the other in order not to waste any time. I do agree with that. The first name you mentioned appeared -- let me say it cautiously, less frequent than the other ones you mentioned. Could you perhaps, as far as the pages are concerned, give me during the first break a small note indicating three or four subsequent words so that we can find them in the transcript of yesterday and see whether there is any problem remaining. Pages and lines disappear on the second day, so if we have to retrieve that on the transcript of yesterday, I need a couple of subsequent words so that we can search for that. If you would give the two during the break, we will check it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Mr. President, have the same -- my own floppy disk, where I registered the texts of yesterday, but I don't think I am authorised to hand it over to you. But if I can, I am at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we try to retrieve the specific places when you give the text. I don't know whether you on your computer, can you view yesterday's transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it on a floppy diskette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it not on your computer, because on my laptop computer at least, I can -- yes, but it is not on your laptop?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is also on the laptop but it is a floppy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have it somewhere in the system with my notes but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will find it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stamp, I think I asked the usher to bring in Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to take advantage of this interval to gain time to tell you that following Mr. Zecevic's testimony, we will tell you how much time we will need to consult with your expert before we start the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you are Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The next of this declaration will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With your leave, Mr. President, may I proceed by handing to the witness the filing of the expert report of the 11th of April, 2002? I trust the Court has copies available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, the -- it is one document with everything in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I see what you are handing to the witness, please? This is it, not this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, may I call you Professor? Is that appropriate?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have in front of you a document which we filed as your statement. Do you see amongst the papers your curriculum vitae in English and the Yugoslav language? [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosnian language"]

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In February, 1994, subsequent to the event at the Markale market on the 5th of February, 1994, were you commissioned by the Court, along with other scientists, to carry out some work and to present a report?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And among the papers, do you see a copy of the report in English and in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is that report to the best of your knowledge, belief, true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the 26th of February, 1996, you gave a statement to officers of the Tribunal, of this Tribunal, explaining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think it is useful to mention this now, because I note that the English transcript does not seem to reproduce the terms used by the Prosecution. It is not a question of meaning but a question of practice that the words be reproduced. A while ago, Mr. Stamp used the word "Yugoslav language," which I heard very clearly and it was translated in the French booth, and I believe that the words should not be transposed in the transcript such as they are stated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where would -- I heard Mr. Stamp saying "B/C/S," but where would he have used the word --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 12 of page 6. I see that everyone is nodding. The word used by Mr. Stamp was "Yugoslav language" and it is not normal that we see "Bosnian language" in the transcript. I don't wish to obstruct anything, I just want the text to be faithful, and since I am listening to both, I wish to underline that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, I think if in the future I reserve to it as the B/C/S language, because I do think I said the Yugoslav language, and probably I said the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Later, you said B/C/S. Mr. Zecevic, "B/C/S" stands for Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian. I think both parties are always trying to use the rather neutral expression, "B/C/S." Sometimes they make a mistake. That happens to both parties. And now and then hear "Yugoslav" or "Bosnian" or "Serbian." I think it is clear to everyone that every party always tries to use the expression "B/C/S." And if one party would fail to do so perhaps at an occasion, it is common understanding that whenever "Yugoslav" is used, that is a reference to "B/C/S."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I note that perfectly and I have nothing against that. What I am trying to say is that it is a technical problem. If a word is pronounced, it must be reflected in the transcript. The transcript cannot interpret our words, whatever they are. It is a question of practice and of principle. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you that in the transcript there should appear the words spoken by counsel. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Professor, I see that you have used the time to peruse the documents more carefully so I could perhaps ask you a composite question. Among those documents, do you see a statement of the 27th of February, 1996 and --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't receive that statement. There must have been some confusion when the documents were handed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please return the papers handed to the witness so that we can see what he actually received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just enquire the Court, does the Court have a copy of the filing dated the 11th of April, 2002?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is all mixed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to be sure what has been handed, can the Prosecution give us all the copies that were given to the witness so as to see to problems that may arise as to date and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Stamp, that you now provided the witness with whatever was in the filing of the 11th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see a record of your statement of the 27th of February, 1996, in English and the B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also records of what you said in interviews that you gave to OTP officials for the 22nd of November, 2001, and the 1st of March, 2002, in both English and B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge and belief, Professor, is the information contained in all five of these documents true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With some perhaps mistakes in translation, but basically everything is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If there is any mistake in translation which you think detracts from the truth or the accuracy of those statements and report to any significant degree, could you please tell us what they are now?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I really have no serious comments to make. I will accept these documents as being truthful, accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There are -- the documents are numbered, Professor, but they are numbered almost in the reverse. I am going to ask you to have a look at page 3450, and that is the handwritten number to the top right of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem. I don't know if it is my microphone or something else. I am experiencing some difficulties. I do not hear one of the channels and I do not also see where do the written numbers appear, at the back, at least. I do not see them, these handwritten numbers. It seems that I do have also -- I am experiencing some technical difficulties at the present time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it your microphone or your earphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to be a technical problem related to earphones. I am going to see if I can stand it by listening to it. I can only hear -- if I listen to only one channel, I can hear correctly but, if not, I shall call somebody to help me. I hear very unpleasant scratchings or -- I hear very unpleasant sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I will ask the technical booth to come in and see whether they could assist you. Can you meanwhile follow what is said so that we can continue? And the handwritten writing is on the top right-hand corner of the pages, as Mr. Stamp explained to us. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, that part of the document is in B/C/S or the -- quite correct, B/C/S. And it is translated at page 3455 into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Professor, in that exposition you explain that the lodging of a tail-fin of a 120-millimetre mortar into the ground depends on certain factors. Now, could you answer orally, please. Don't nod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if you nod, the interpreters who are sitting, not in front of you, they cannot translate that and it cannot be put into the transcript. So, therefore, if you are nodding yes, would you please pronounce the word "yes," and if you are nodding no, would you please pronounce the word "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in your report, you indicated that the tail-fin at the Markale market explosion on the 5th of February, 1994, had been lodged to some degree into the asphalt ground of the market?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I know, Professor, it is highly scientific, but I am going to ask you to explain again the proposition that you have here, slowly and carefully, so that the Court could understand the significance of the lodging of the 120-millimetre mortar fin in the asphalt ground of the market on the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The projectile, mortar projectile, when it hits a target, in this case it hit the asphalt surface of the market under an angle of 60, of approximately 60 degrees with respect to the ground level. Upon hitting, there was fragmentation of the body of the projectile. The result of the fragmentation is the following: The jacket of the mortar changed into or became fragmented and these fragments spread very quickly around in the surrounding area, however, the stabiliser that was part of the last part of the body of the mortar, almost -- it never fragments; it never bursts into small pieces, into fragments. And in this particular case, the stabiliser continued its trajectory towards the ground and embedded itself in a depth of approximately 250 millimeters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, every word you speak has to be translated. If you slow down the speed of your speech, the interpreters will be better able to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in fact, in the transcript that I can follow now, only now I see at "250 millimetres," and where I listened to the French booth, I heard "250 kilometres." This is what I seem to hear. I guess the depth and the speed was of some sort of a confusion here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not speak of the speed of the mortar. Velocity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are talking about the depth of approximately 250 millimetres and--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was translated in "kilometres" in French, and that is what Mr. Piletta-Zanin tries to draw our attention to. But, of course, it would create no confusion. No one would ever think of a tail-fin, a stabiliser, to go 250 kilometres in the ground. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order for the stabiliser to be embedded into the asphalt service at a depth of 250 millimetres, [Realtime transcript read in error "kilometres"] the stabiliser has to have a certain impact velocity, a certain energy. At the time of the explosion, the mortar already had its arrival velocity, the arrival to the target. When the explosion occurred, the detonation caused that the surface of the stabiliser was affected with a certain velocity which had to result from -- it had to result that the stabiliser should hit upwards, but since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...assist you, I know that again kilometres and millimetres are -- I think, as a matter of fact, I think that the witness was misled by our discussion and used these words, but I am not quite sure. If you would look at your screen. Once the cursor stops moving, you may continue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I ask you one or two questions. You said --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- that the body of the mortar fragments and the stabiliser does not fragment?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The stabiliser, you said, continues in its path of approach?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under certain circumstances, of course. It depends of the velocity at the point of impact and the explosion. If the velocity of the mortar is of a certain value, it can occur that the stabiliser flows backwards or bounces back near the explosion impact and can also go right into the ground. But in this case, the stabiliser hit the surface and got itself embedded into it. I can talk to you about my experience. My previous experience shows that at the time of the explosion, at the moment of the explosion, the force of the product created by the detonation makes it so that the stabiliser is thrown back at a distance of 150 metres per second plus/minus 20 metres per second. 170 metres per second, correction. If we think that -- if we actually look at the calculations that were made, it can show that the energy in which the stabiliser hit the ground -- penetrated the ground --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this witness is talking way too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave already a sign to the witness that he should slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I wish to say is that the transcript, the English transcript, shows distance instead of speed, and this is fundamental. And if I am doing this, it is to help everybody inside this courtroom. There is a big difference between the word "distance" and "velocity." The witness said "velocity." I hear that he said that. He is nodding. And I think the Prosecution should also verify what appears on the transcript. I cannot do their work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could have repeated that part because if you talk too quickly, especially when it is very technical language, it might be easily not followed by the interpreters. So may I ask your attention to that again. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do not bother at all if you make a correction to the transcript for the better understanding, but you started saying "if the witness talks too quickly," I mean, that was clear to everyone. And if you would then immediately go to where the transcript failed to reflect the words of the expert witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Professor, in your report, you said: As a round approaches earth, it falls at a velocity determined by the level of the charge.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what you mean by that, please

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A mortar bomb can reach certain targets and fall under certain angles, depending on the elevation, and it also depends of the level of the charge. Each additional charge determines the initial speed of the mortar. If the additional charge is greater, the velocity of the mortar shell is greater. In this case, if we talk about 120-millimetre M-6253 shell, there are six additional charges which means that -- means that the difference between the beginning, the velocity, the initial velocity, initial speed, goes from 140 up to 170 metres per second, depending on the additional charge -- no, I am not saying "170" but 310. It goes from 140 to 310 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So can I take it from what you are saying that, at charge 1, the initial velocity would be approximately 140 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The velocity of the launch, however, when the projectile falls, it is lesser, the velocity is lesser.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at charge 6, the initial velocity would be greater and would be how much, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 310 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, does the initial velocity have a consequence on the impact velocity? That is, when the mortar arrives on target, does it affect it at all?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it has a direct effect. If the initial velocity is greater, generally speaking, the impact velocity is greater. This proportion is not a linear proportion but it is lesser, it is lesser than the initial velocity. It also depends on the angle from which the shell is launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now when the shell explodes on contact with the ground, you say the body of the shell fragments but the tail-fin does not. Is there a force from the explosion which tends to push the shell backward from the centre of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, not the projectile, but the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. And what is -- could you describe the degree of that force of the explosion which is tending to push the stabiliser fin backward?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the velocity is contrary to the -- is approximately 150 plus/minus 20 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am terribly sorry. There is a word that was not written down and it is very important that we see what it is contrary to. Line 4 in the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer was, as we read it in the English transcript: "Well, the velocity is contrary to the -- " Could you please fill in that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That velocity is 170 metres plus/minus 20. Not 150 but 170 plus/minus 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it is contrary to what --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Inertia [Realtime transcript read in error "inushera"] of the shell. The mass of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you mean contrary to the mass of the shell or to the stabiliser fin?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will explain. Upon impact of the shell, the shell has its own inertia, its velocity. At the moment of the explosion, the products of the detonation react to the front of the stabiliser and they kick the stabiliser away, they push it backwards. If there was no explosion, the mine would continue to travel towards the ground and it will embed itself in the ground. But in this case, the detonation makes it so that it is pushed backwards. So whether the stabiliser will be pushed back or whether the stabiliser will be embedded in the ground, it depends upon the velocity of the shell upon its arrival, upon its -- upon the impact point. So the velocity of the two at the moment of impact is the same. I can also try to explain it to you by making a sketch. Maybe the visual effect will be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you please do so, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If a clear piece of paper could be given to the witness and perhaps put on the ELMO so that we can follow what he draw. Yes. You perhaps turn the ELMO in such a way that it is comfortable for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to say at this very moment that, on line 17, just to make sure, we are not talking about "inushera" but "inertia," and since the word is not written correctly, we just like the appropriate modifications to be brought to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perfect issue for the yellow papers, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment, upon arrival of the shell and upon its hitting the ground, it obtains its velocity. The velocity is "V." This velocity depends on the additional charge, the amount of the additional charge that was used, and also it depends on the elevation. This is the angle under which -- the descent angle of the mortar, and it is approximately 60 degrees. It is the descent angle. Right after that, when the detonation occurs, the shell becomes broader. And after the detonation, because we hear -- the explosion charges are right here. So what happens is that the explosion charges tend to destroy the metal jacket of -- the metal body of the shell. So the pressure that is -- the pressure inside is 1.100 bars and the temperature is 2.500 Celsius degrees. 2.500 Celsius. At that moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just put your initial and the number 1 on that document which you have just drawn on, please. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the body of the mine fragments, the shell fragments, and it fragments into many fragment pieces, they scatter in the surrounding distance at a distance of approximately 1.000 metres per second. However, the front of the stabiliser has some forces. The forces, the pressure of the products of the detonation, affect the stabiliser and this is why the stabiliser wants to be pushed back. And this is -- and the stabiliser still has the same velocity at this point. So the stabiliser also has the velocity which is equal to the velocity of the impact point, and the products of the detonation are also reacting towards or acting towards this stabiliser. And this velocity here, according to some calculations, shows that it should be approximately 170 plus/minus 20 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop. Explain to us again what is 170 plus/minus 20 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is the velocity with which the products of the detonation tend to push back the stabiliser, to push it back contrary to its path towards the ground. So they act upon the stabiliser. So we have the velocity of the arrival, "V", minus this "VD", velocity. The stabiliser can at that particular moment, depending on the value of this velocity here -- if this velocity is smaller than 170 metres per second, what will happen is the following: The stabiliser will be pushed back from the impact point. It will fall near the centre of the explosion, in the vicinity of the centre. If the velocity of arrival is equal to 170 metres per second, the stabiliser will be embedded right into the centre of the explosion. If "V" here is greater than 170, the stabiliser will at that point tend to embed itself into the ground. In this particular case, we have found that the body of the stabiliser was embedded into the ground, which means that the shell, for sure, had a velocity, the impact velocity of 170 plus/minus 20, or its velocity was greater than the 170 plus/minus 20 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am going to ask you to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the shell that you found embedded to that degree or that was embedded to the degree it was embedded at Markale, would have had to have an approach velocity in excess of what?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of 170 plus/minus 20 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Further calculations showed -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We will get to the further calculations. I am going to ask you to go over this again, and I am going to put some propositions to you and you will tell me if I am right or I am wrong. The 120-millimetre mortar that was fired into Markale market can be fired from six charges. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The greater the charge used between 1 to 6 charge is a higher --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am terribly, terribly sorry. I must intervene at this point. I believe hearing the French booth say that it was bearing six charges, whereas the question was more to the effect that it can possess six charges. And I believe that this distinction is very important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is what, at least, in the English language understood the witness said, and which is also logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the greater the charge, the greater the impact velocity?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On explosion, the products of explosion tend to be pressing outwards and pushing back the stabiliser at 170 metres per second plus/minus 20 metres per second. Correct? Don't nod, please.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the stabiliser will be pushed back if its approach velocity is less than 170 metres per second plus/minus 20 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That situation would fall somewhere near to the centre of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It would only continue on its path and penetrate the ground if it is approaching at faster than 170 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And for it to approach the ground at faster than 170 metres per second and lodge to the degree it did, from what you saw in Markale market, at approximately what charge would it have had to be fired?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am objecting. I object to this question, for the following reasons. They are technical reasons. I believe that, depending on the distance as well, that everything depended on the distance and since distance is not established, this type of question seems to be a question that is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...answer the question instead of making an objection to the question. If the question is such that it could not be answered unless there would be other information available, the witness will tell us. And during cross-examination, you are fully entitled to -- So, please proceed, Mr. Stamp. Your objection is denied. And I must ask you not to interfere when it is not a real objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question, and I repeat the question: For the stabiliser fin and the mortar to approach the ground at Markale at a speed faster than 170 metres per second and lodge to the degree it did as you saw at Markale, at approximately what charge would it have had to be fire?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It would have to have been fired with a fourth, fifth and sixth charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your report and your statement indicates that you took into consideration the topography of the Markale -- of the Sarajevo area --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Type of --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you found the angle of descent was 55 to 65 degrees?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having regard to all those factors, how far would that mortar be if it had been fired on the fourth, fifth or sixth charge, approximately how far?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That distance is between 4.900 to 6.000 metres, considering this angle and the depth of penetration of 250 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it possible that the -- it could have been fired from charge 3?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It could have been fired, but these -- this situation could not have occurred on the ground, that is, the penetration depth of 250 millimetres. That is the key reason. For the stabiliser to be lodged at a depth of 250 millimetres into the ground, it would have had, at the time of penetration, to have had a velocity of 60 plus/minus 10 metres per second. Since this 60 metres per second, plus this velocity of 170 plus/minus 20 metres per second, shows that the shell must have had at the moment of impact a minimum velocity of 200 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, that is very informative. But if I could get back to the question. Is it possible that it could have been fired from charge 3? Do I take the answer to be "no" or "unlikely" or "probably," or what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Charge 2?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Charge 1?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it had been fired from charge 1, would the impact velocity be more than 170 metres per second?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The impact velocity would have been about 110 to 120 metres per second, depending on the angle of decent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it from your previous answers that had it been fired on charges 2 or 3, the impact velocity would not have been sufficient for it to lodge into the ground?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for it to lodge 250 metres deep into the ground. Millimetres, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said in your report that your conclusions were to some degree based on and confirmed by research done by one Miroljub Vukasinovic at the Belgrade Military Institute. You said that in your report?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Belgrade Military Institute, could you just tell us quickly what the Belgrade Military Institute is in respect to the 120-millimetre mortar? If you could in a sentence.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Belgrade Military Institute of the Grad Forces in Belgrade is a highly respectful scientific institution that before the war, and probably still now, does research for the needs of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, formally the Yugoslav People's Army, and that institution also started projectiles of 120 millimetres and mortars of 120 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it that includes the Yugoslav 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of the pre-former Yugoslavia because that mortar was manufactured in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That mortar was manufactured in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is what you just said. Which mortar are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mortar weapons are produced by the Bratstvo factory in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The shells as projectiles of 120 millimetres were manufactured at Pretis, a factory in the immediate vicinity of Sarajevo, Licki Osik, a factory in Kraijina, in Lika, and Krusik Valjevo, a factory in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We will get back to that, Professor. Subsequent to the time before today when you last spoke with the OTP --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I simply have no more translation. The question -- Mr. Stamp's question was not translated for me, at least I didn't hear it at all. I heard the answer but I did not get the question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous question or the last one which -- I take it that you are talking about the question that has been answered by the witness, which reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is perfect. But I think it was not translated in any event. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last question that was answered by the witness was: "That mortar was manufactured in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what you just said. Which mortar are you referring to?" That was the question. So I take it that it is now translated. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is not good of my -- of my answer on the transcript. The line is 25.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness said is that it was not translated well. That is what the interpreter said, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if the witness says that it is not properly translated, that is translated by the interpreters to ask. So we know what he just said, and I was just to invite him to correct what was not properly translated. Could you please do so, Mr. Zecevic. Would you please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mortar weapons were produced in the Bratstvo factory and the shell as a projectile was manufactured in Pretis, a factory close to Sarajevo, or in a factory in Licki Osik, in Lika, Krajina or in the Krusik factory in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very sorry, Mr. President. It is because the French translation said in relation to what this witness just said that the answer was not good. The witness did not say, "My answer was not good." He said, "It was not translated well." I think we have to be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that has been clarified now. Please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in your report, if I may lay the foundation to where I am going, you said in your report that your conclusions were based on your own studies and studies done by Miroslav [sic] Vukasinovic of the Belgrade Military Institute. Now --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- since you spoke to us and gave us that information, have you obtained any further information in respect to that proposition of the charges effecting the lodging of the shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The report of Dr. Vukasinovic is based mostly on scientific thinking in Russia regarding explosion physics. It is very interesting and a highly valuable document. However, I conducted analysis of research done in the United States, the ballistics laboratory, and I used their research results to estimate the value of the velocity of rejection and the velocity of the penetration of the stabiliser into the soil. There are certain differences in values, but they are of the same order of magnitude. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but slowly, if you can. Please proceed. You may continue, but I was indicating if you could do so slowly.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I am rather emotional so I speak quickly. According to Dr. Vukasinovic, the velocity of rejection is about 160 metres per second, due to the effect of detonation products. And this value that he used or borrowed from a Russian scientist, I used equations obtained from Sukas and Walters. They mention velocity of 170 plus/minus 20 metres per second as the tolerance and I adopted this because of the seriousness of this Tribunal. There is no possibility, however, of defining this with precision. You can't say it is 143 or 173. There has to be a certain range of reliability of this value. To determine the velocity of penetration into the ground, I used the well-known formulas that exist for 150 years and that were established by French scientists during the wars of nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and those formulas are extremely reliable. And it is with the help of those that I did establish that the necessary velocity for penetration into the ground to a depth of 250 millimetres is of the order of 60 plus/minus 10 metres per second. Those formulas can be found in any serious textbook on munitions, and the basis is certainly the well-known French scientist who published a book, "The Construction of Ammunitions."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So, finally, may I ask you, in coming to your conclusions, you have considered the report of the Belgrade Military Institute who were involved in designing the 120-millimetre mortar? The Russians, the Russian scientist --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is the Yugoslav 120-millimetre mortar based on any previous mortar? Is it designed from any previous mortar that was being used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, but it seems to me that I am the only one following the transcript. The witness indicated the name of the French expert, and I think it is important. Could we ask him to repeat it? I think he said Mr. Saterline, and the name doesn't appear in the transcript. And I think that these things should appear on the transcript

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you could understand, could the witness repeat the name of the French scientist, that would have taken one line and a half. Now it took you five lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am sorry for that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was the Yugoslav 120-millimetre designed from a previous mortar that was in use?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. The 120-millimetre mortar M-62 was developed on the basis of a heavy Russian mortar, M-52, I think it is. But by design it is an original Yugoslav design. And it is a standard type of mortar, standard mortar shell, worldwide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And you considered the research and work on mortar ballistics of the Belgrade Military Institute, the Russian scientists, the French scientists and the American scientists, and your own research; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having regard to the time, Mr. President, Your Honours, I will not go into certain aspects of what he has to say. The report and the statements are in evidence. He has mentioned certain things about the make of the shell that fell in the market, and if I may invite Your Honours to -- well, I am quite sure that Your Honours will have a look at the entire report. But the explanations are in the report and I leave it now to my friend and the Court. That is the examination-in-chief, may it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. How much time would the Defence need to prepare for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, until the break that we have at the usual time, the Defence would like to ask a couple of questions that are not linked to this report, some more general questions. And if we can have the time from 10.30 to 11.30, the Defence would need that time for my colleague Piletta and myself to consult our expert, and then we would start the cross-examination within the time allowed us by Your Honours for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you would stay, if we would resume at 12.30, and since we have time until a quarter to 2.00. Yes, of course, 11.30, from 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until 1345. That would be a bit over two hours. But, of course, there might be questions from the Bench as well. There might be need to re-examine the witness. So I said yesterday, not more than two hours. May I just ask you, Mr. Zecevic, if necessary, would you still be available after today? We are trying to finish today, but if it would turn out to be necessary to continue next week, would you still be available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am at your disposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Although we try to finish, but it is an important issue and therefore we should not -- we should not try to do it too quickly. Yes, please proceed, now, with your general questions, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, good afternoon. I am sorry, good morning. In your curriculum vitae that you provided to the Tribunal, and talking to the investigators of the Prosecution, you said that you wrote a thesis entitled "The Effect of Variable Fields of High Radical Acceleration on the Internal Ballistics of Rocket Engines with Special Types of Fuel." Can you confirm that this was a doctoral thesis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm -- can you confirm that this was a doctoral thesis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your tutor?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Ejub Ganic, who during the conflict in 1992, 1993, and 1994, held very high positions and replaced Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he replaced him. I don't remember, but he is the person I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your biography, you confirmed that you were one of the ten greatest experts for weaponry in the former Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As an expert, and you are one of the ten greatest experts, were you the winner of the national awards?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which country?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were one of the greatest experts in the former Yugoslavia and in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not win any awards.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You acquired your doctoral degree on the basis of the thesis, the name of which we have mentioned. Does that mean that you did not specialise in mortar shells, but rocket projectiles?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what research you did into mines? Were you more active with regard to mortar shells or rocket projectiles?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I give an elaborated answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if you could please just answer my question, which you devoted more attention to.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By my basic orientation, I was an ammunition designer. I worked for 20 years in a factory for the production of ammunition. I am the only designer of the 128-millimetre rocket, M-87, which was an original design: the rocket engine, the warhead, the design of the projectile, the testing. I also worked on a propagation mine of 120 millimetre. I also worked on 129-millimetre, a 50-millimetre rocket, the whole design of that rocket, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you worked in production?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, not in production, but in a factory manufacturing ammunitions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict in Sarajevo - I am talking of the period 1992, 1993, and 1994 - you told the investigators that you had executive control over the production of ammunition for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not executive control. I was head of the research and development department.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is too fast, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you both to make a pause between question and answer and then answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I have in front of me some additional information which the Defence received from the Prosecution, and in the translation, it said that during the conflict, you had executive control over the department for the production of ammunition for the BH army. Maybe it hasn't been correctly translated. Would you explain what your role was?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the 1992/1993 period, I was head of the research and development department attached to the centre for special production in the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My task was to try, in view of the shortages and no import of ammunition, no electricity, and no sources of energy, no explosives --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My question was a simple one: What was your position? Can you please confirm that what you told the investigators?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the witness is now explaining what it is and it seems, as far as I understand from what you quoted, to be different from what is in that statement. And the witness may explain. He explained already what his position was. If you say it is important to know what his task was, and usually positions and tasks are both of importance, the witness could finish his answer. If you would say that since he now explains his position, that would be enough, then we don't need any further information about the tasks he performed in that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I think that the witness was explaining the conditions prevailing at the time, and which put him in a position as to hold the position of manager that he held. I just wanted the witness to confirm his -- what exact position he held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said that his position was that he was head of the research and development department attached to the centre for special production in the Main Staff. When he started explaining his task, I think he described the circumstances under which the necessity for performing this task became apparent. I think his position has been explained. If that is just what you wanted to know, I think the question has been answered. And it is different from what you quoted from his statement. That is clear to everyone as well. Ms. Pilipovic, looking at the clock, it is a couple of minutes. If you would say "I continue for just a couple of minutes -- "

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then with the assistance with the interpreters, we could continue for a couple of minutes and then have a longer break. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us, please, where the factory for the production of the ammunition was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have a factory for the production of ammunition. We had small workshops for the production of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that one of those factories was in Alipasino Polje, which factory for the production of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I explain in some detail? In Sarajevo there were at the same time, two lines: One line next to the Ministry of Energy, where the Pretis factory was, and it manufactured ammunition. I am talking to the part of Pretis that was within Sarajevo. Another organisation that I was in was a purely military organisation. It was not under civilian control, and it manufactured in wartime workshops and partly through ordering material from certain factories. Therefore, within Sarajevo, in 1992 and 1993, there were two parallel cycles of production, one under the control of the civilian authorities and the other under the control of the military authorities. That is where I was, and I can tell you more about that because I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I think what Ms. Pilipovic would like to know is whether there was either a factory, perhaps, or a workshop in Alipasino Polje. I think that is what the question was about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we would start at 11.30, would that be good? Then we will adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, before the break, you told us that the production of mortars took place in Alipasino Polje --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that this was the case, that the mortars were manufactured in Alipasino Polje. It is you that said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your interview with the investigators, the 7th and 10th of September, 2000, you said that mortars were manufactured in a casting plate in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you are saying that shells were manufactured in Alipasino Polje, can you tell us what sort of shells, what was their calibre, the ones manufactured in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is a casting plant in Alipasino Polje where casts were made for mortars of 82 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when the manufacturing starting, and can you please tell us where the plant was?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the manufacturing started in November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please slow down? Especially, Mr. Zecevic, you and Ms. Pilipovic are speaking the same language, and that always causes additional problems. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I take advantage --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to say that there will be a persistent problem, but I will continue in this way. I heard from the French booth that there were mortars of 128 millimetres. That is what I heard. In the transcript, it says "82 millimetres." So we have to see which of the two figures is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said: "Casts were made in Alipasino Polje for mortars," was it of 82 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us -- you said, in fact, that manufacturing started in November 1992. Can you tell us with accuracy where the plant was in Alipasino Polje exactly, the exact location?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What is -- what is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the English booth is getting the French translation. I don't know what is happening. There is an echo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there is an echo for everyone, and give me an opportunity first to react, and if I do not, please interfere. We have a technical problem, I think, since we have different translations on different channels. I have got on channel 4 now the French translation. I think we get it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the B/C/S booth hears the French translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the interpreters tell us what is happening in their view because I see some signs. It seems that now I don't hear any French translation any more. So everything has been solved. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when you are saying "Alipasino Polje," can you tell us the street where the manufacturing plant was?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said "no," and then you started saying because in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is not so important.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it because you do not know or you do not wish to answer?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the war started in the former Yugoslavia, all the names of the streets changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Zecevic, do you know the name of an old street or a new street, and have you been there? Could you locate the spot? You are nodding. May I take it that your answer is "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I can pinpoint where the manufacturing plant was. I believe that before the war the street was called Dzemal Bijedic Street. I don't know what its name is currently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you told us that there were several workshops where manufacturing took place. Could you tell us in which parts of the city were the workshops located?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you because this work did not fall within the scope of my action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether you know it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You said you did not know because it did not fall within the scope of your activities. I am talking about make-shift manufacturing. But what about the BH army? Can you tell us, since you knew where the production plants were, the casting plants were?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was only one line, it was in Alipasino Polje. When I speak about workshops, well, I here understand small workshops with one or two machines. So where I was, there were only a few machines which were scattered throughout Sarajevo. The part of them which I was able to see was at the mechanical engineering faculty where I was employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say they were scattered all over Sarajevo, can you tell us in what sort of buildings were those workshops housed?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did not deal in manufacturing. I was -- I dealt with development and research. Other peoples were in charge of that aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether you know where these workshops were housed, in what kind of buildings? If you know tell us. If you don't know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you, as an expert, did not visit or supervise the production?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you did a study as member of the commission for the incidents -- for the incident at the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us from whom did you hear about the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I saw it on the news programme of the Bosnian television.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you saw on the news programme of the Bosnian television?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I saw a footage of the event, that is, what followed the event, and I heard different statements made by responsible persons, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you saw footages of the event following the event, can you tell us what you saw on that footage? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many people were there helping the wounded, putting them in cars, taking them away, their comments. That is all I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statements, you said that you saw a French soldier?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on television we saw the moment when a French soldier was digging up a part of the stabiliser and was taking it out of the ground. It was a very short clip of that footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how can you describe what the clip was? Can you describe it in relation to the area where the crater was dug out, as you say?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The sequence lasted one or one and-a-half seconds. And as far as I can remember, that is all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the sequence, what could you see which lasted a very short time? What could you see?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I saw a soldier and some people who were crouching around the centre of the explosion, and this soldier tries to take out the stabiliser. And that was all one could see at that moment, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Your study was composed also by three other members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who appointed you and when to be a member of that commission?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Judge Asim Kanovic, I think. He appointed me. It was on February 6, 1994. On the previous day, on February 5th, I called my acquaintance who worked as the head of the crime department at the Sarajevo police and told him that one should approach the problem of the explosion seriously because, on that very same evening, there was much confusion in the statements of individual people. He asked me to come the next day to the Markale market. I went there. I met the investigating judge. I told him in brief what my occupation was, what my colleague's occupation was, and he appointed us on the spot to be part of the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, as far as I can gather from what you have just said, you were the one who formed the commission, proposed the commission?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I proposed the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On February 5th, when you heard about the incident, did you go there on the spot?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The place where I live and the place where the incident took place is at a distance of 7 millimetres -- "no" is the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pilipovic, if you speak at the same time, it even becomes more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask for other earphones because I have problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...ask for other earphones. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you said that you proposed who would be in the commission?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was in charge of the work of the commission?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the task of the commission was which you headed?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The task was to try to determine the cause of the massacre in Markale.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand you, on February 6th, you came to the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the crater that was allegedly made from the remnants of the stabiliser of the mortar?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The crater doesn't -- is not caused by the remnants of the stabiliser but by the explosion, and the hole in which the stabiliser was is quite a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you photograph that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not me, but I asked that this should be photographed because I did -- I was not authorised to take photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you asked photographs to be taken, to photograph everything on the site, does that mean that on February 6th, you had persons with you who was a photographer and who photographed?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I only was -- I was only able to convey this. No, I didn't have anyone with me. I just asked that this should be done. And I was told that photographs had been taken the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, on that day when you went with the other two members of the commission, that you didn't have a photographer with you and you had taken no photos that day?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We did take photos, the things that I encircled, but I was not in charge of that. I could only express the wish to have a photographer, and this wish was fulfilled because the photographer was a police photographer. I was not authorised to know who the person was. I only said that photographs would be necessary, and photographs were taken of the area which I encircled with chalk.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on February 6th, you had with you a person who took photographs of this site of what you asked to be photographed?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the person was?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I saw him only once. And it wasn't very important as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you are saying that this person was not important for you, does that mean that you didn't use the photographs that the photographer had taken on that day, if he took photographs?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Don't distort my answer. Don't distort my statement. I used the photographs that I received from the police, that what I asked to be photographed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, does that mean that the persons who -- that the person who photographed on February 6th what you encircled that should be photographed, was a person who was employed by the police?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you. I don't have accurate information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How can you explain that in response to my question when I asked about the photographs, that they were given to you by someone from the police?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, people from the police brought me those photographs, and who they engaged as the photographer, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us when you received photographs from that person who, on February 6th, photographed the site of the incident?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I received the photographs the next day on the 7th of February, if I can recollect it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor did you measure the angle of penetration of the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked to be brought the remnants of the stabiliser. And then at the place of the centre of the explosion, I spotted a hole which the stabiliser had penetrated on the previous day. I put the remnants of the stabiliser in the hole, and thanks to -- and with the aid of a quadrant on the basis of which you can determine the angle, I determined the angle of the front of the stabiliser in the part where the capsule is and the basic charge is. This is one way of doing it. I also measured the depth of the opening in which the carrier of the stabiliser was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Since you say that you measured the angle of the penetration of the stabiliser, you asked to tell us how it was done. Can you confirm to us whether you photographed the moment when the angle was ascertained on that day since you had the photographer with you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you photograph the crater?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether those photographs that were made on that day, were they used for writing the study that you were in charge of doing?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The photographs were not a basis for writing the report but some of the photographs had been included in that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that you used a part of the photographs that were -- that had been used for the report?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Look at page 3482.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I looked at this. I just wanted confirmation if these were photographs of the 6th of February. Professor, you told us that when you came to the scene, that you asked that the stabiliser be brought to you.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you were informed that the stabiliser had been taken out?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was not informed of this. When I came to the site, I saw that there was no stabiliser there, and I asked where it was. And I was told that it had been taken out by a soldier, a UN soldier, and I asked that it be brought so that I could try to reconstruct the attack angle of the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From whom did you ask to have the stabiliser brought to you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From the judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the judge told you where the stabiliser exactly was?
