utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. This was not within the scope of my activity and there was no need to ask the judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the judge tell you precisely who had taken the stabiliser and where?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who brought the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on February 6th, you say that you did not know who brought the stabiliser. Can you tell us for how long did you use the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say at this moment for how long I used it. Perhaps a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were using this stabiliser and while you were doing the investigation, was the judge with you all that time?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most of the time. I didn't pay attention to this, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, was a report made?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand who is to write down the minutes. I registered information on my own and I have a record of the results of my investigations. And on that -- on the basis of that material, I wrote my report. I, as an expert authorised by the Court, at least as far as I was informed, I had no more precise instructions that I had to do anything in addition.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were working for yourself?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I wrote down my own notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You wrote notes for yourself. The investigating judge, did he keep records of what was going on that day?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was authorised from the judge to receive report in two, two and-a-half days at the most, and according to his instruction, my report was only reliable, that is, the commission, the three of us who were in that commission, all three of us were engaged in writing the report and in preparing the material for writing the report, which implied that we had to make a detailed investigation of the site of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when you went on site that day, did you also find the remnants of the body of the shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked that fragments be found, and according to the information that I received at the time, I know that they were only able to find two fragments. Because the previous day, after the incident that occurred, there was a lot of blood on the market. In the afternoon hours, the firemen came on to the spot and they also proceeded to cleaning the area with very strong water hoses, so that is the reason why most of these fragments were also cleaned out or disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, therefore, you are answering to us that you did not find shrapnels of the body on the site?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If an explosion occurred correctly, you don't really find remnants. There are just fragments that fly at a very high speed, a few thousand metres per second, and it is very difficult to find bigger metal fragments belonging to the body of the shell on the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, regarding these fragments for which you say that usually they stay on the spot, were you able to find any fragments on the site?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I only told you that I found two. Two fragments were found and they were given to the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that on the 6th of February, you only found two fragments?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the previous day, therefore, on the 5th of February, was there a team that went out on site, a team belonging to the centre of the Security Services?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was not informed of that at that point. However, at a later stage, I found out that fact over the television. In fact, that was not long ago, when I was following this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is it that you heard exactly?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That there was an on-site investigation belonging to the police department and they went to carry out an on-site investigation, and that is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At that time did you hear that that team found shrapnels belonging to the shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And that they were the ones who took away the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, you do not know and you never saw shrapnels that were found on site on the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I told you that two were found. Two fragments, two shrapnel fragments.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you carry out some lab examinations?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding these two fragments?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, it was to make a report and I had two days to do it. In fact, better to say I had 30 hours to complete my report. In Sarajevo at the time, there was no electricity, there was no water, there was no fuel for transportation. It was impossible for any type of analysis to be done. We could not carry out the metallic analysis of these shrapnels. We had to use a very sophisticated laboratory which was not available at the time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I know that in Sarajevo there was a war. I only asked you if you carried out some analysis. Do you know if at any point in time there was any kind of analysis carried out on the shrapnels?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, after I drafted this report, nobody ever, aside from members of the OTP, contacted me to talk about this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on that day when you were using the stabiliser, can you tell us, after you finished your part of the work, if you will, who -- did somebody take away the stabiliser and who took it away?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was not particularly interested by that fact because it is out of the scope of my activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us which parts of the projectile were you able to analyse during the identification of the projectile, or to examine, to look at?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I only had the carrier of the stabiliser, madam, and it is on this carrier that you were able to see embedded the charges, initial charges, with the capsules. And according to this, I was able to identify the type of projectile and the type of the capsule, also the type of the initial charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, can you tell us what led you to believe that it was the charge that was used, in fact?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were able to conclude that the shell was filled with ammunition and powder?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who is the manufacturer?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was Krusik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what were you able to conclude this?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because of the standard marks that are embedded on the initial charge, and it is also the standard procedure regarding ammunition for the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Aside from the fact that it was written on it "Krusik Valjevo," what else was embedded? What else were you able to read on that part?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was also M-74 capsule, the year of the manufacturing also was there, and it was 1996, with regards to the initial charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: M-74. Can you please tell us where are those parts?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How do you want me to tell you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the translation says that it was 1996. Is that what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I heard --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in 1987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, how do you want me to know where they were? They were out of the scope of my work. I didn't find them, and I answered to your previous question I don't know where they were brought. But there was -- the initial charge was there into the carrier of the stabiliser and the capsule was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell us what was the material with which the body of the shell was produced?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was made out of steel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, can you describe to us what the surface of the ground of the Markale market looked like? Can you explain to us and tell us what the structure of the ground?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was a layer of asphalt, probably two centimetres thick, and the underneath there was sand and small rocks, gravel, small stones.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: According to your expertise, could you tell us what was the firmness of that layer?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am not a geologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I believe that you told us that you measured the depth of the crater of which allegedly was formed by the shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the depth, please?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From 200 to 250 millimetres, depending on the angle, depending on what end of the hole you measure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it depends on the part that you measure, can you be a little bit more precise?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can only make a drawing, if you wish, a sketch. You will understand then. Because like this, it is a bit difficult to explain

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, if we could allow the Professor to draw a sketch.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in fact, it is perhaps not really important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no difficulty in understanding what the witness said. But if you would like to use your time to make him draw, then, of course, it is up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you very much. It won't be necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when you said that you measured the depth of the crater, would you be able to tell us if the measurement was made starting from the upper layer of the surface of the asphalt?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As that part of the asphalt was missing, so we placed a stick, and on the basis of that, many measurements were carried out in order to attain this figure of 200 to 250 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you held the stabiliser, you had it in your hands? Were you able to measure also the length?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Of the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you also able to measure the -- sir, the width of the crater?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the dimensions? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if the crater had the same width all along the hole in the depth?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we understand each other. What do you mean by "width"?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, there is a crater which had its depth. When you were measuring the width of the crater --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I measured the girth or the area of the explosion, and when I measured this space in which the explosion occurred, there was also a place where the asphalt was destroyed, and there is also a part where the asphalt was not destroyed but some parts of particles of the asphalt were removed, were blown away. So we can see where the -- where the impact occurred under a great deal of velocity and these fragments hit the asphalt and ricocheted. So this is what I want you to precise. I know what the dimensions were; I have them in my notes. But I couldn't tell you by heart. I could consult my notes, if you wish. I would then be able to give you precise figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. If it is necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I ask you, wouldn't there be some confusion? You are using the word "crater" while what we were talking about was the tunnel. And I think you wanted to know the dimensions, the diameter, I would say, of the tunnel, rather than of the crater. You used the word "crater," where the witness indicated before that the crater is something different from the hole or tunnel. So perhaps if you put the question differently, you would get the answer you would like.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you also ask the counsel and the witness to speak slower, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I ask you also to speak slower, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the width of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: About 40 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, would you be able to confirm to us if when the shell is activated, at the precise moment of the explosion, the explosive force, the force of explosion, if I may use that term, does it clear the area surrounding the crater?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It all depends on the type of fuse, if the fuse is set to a super-rapid action or if it is set to start later. If the surface is very strong, it also depends on that. So many factors depend on the -- on what will happen after the explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I also ask one more question. You said the diameter, I understand, of the tunnel was 40 millimetres. At least, that is 40 millimetres, so 4 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very briefly, I must do it really at this point. I read in the English transcript, "type of fuse," which is type of detonator and not type of terrain, which we find in the French interpretation. So I would like this to be corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I heard in the English translation. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when a mine -- a bomb explodes, around that area where the explosion took place, what happens with the objects that surround that area? Are they pushed away?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a metre to a metre and-a-half around the place of explosion, the impact, upon the pressure that occurs after, that you see the sort of a -- the intensity, and depending on the objects that are surrounding that area, these objects can be pushed away, blown away, or not. It all depends on the mass of the surface. Of the structure as well, if it is a metal structure, if it is a wooden structure. It is a very complex question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, is it possible that upon the explosion and after the stabiliser embedded itself on the ground, into the ground, is it possible that a crater be formed and that the stabiliser be completely embedded inside and that you do not see where the crater is and you don't see the stabiliser, either, on that very strong asphalt surface, for instance? Would you please be able to explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you talking about the crater or are you talking about the tunnel or the hole?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about the crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat again. It really all depends on the type of fuse. If the fuse is set to act, react immediately, the shell will practically detonate immediately after -- upon contact with a surface. And it has -- if it didn't happen that way, the efficiency would not -- the military efficiency or the military purpose of this would not be interesting. There are fuses which are set to detonate slower. Then in that case, the shell goes right into the obstacle, and at that point, they react inside the surface and the hole -- the consequence of everything would be quite different. In this particular case, it is quite clear that the fuse was set to impact immediately. It is a super quick fuse, as we call it. And the effect that it caused on to the surface, it really all depends on the quality of the terrain, on the thickness of the asphalt as well, of the firmness, of the consistency of the ground, and also it depends on the velocity of the shell. And all these factors influence the depth. So it is a very complex issue and it is not very easy to answer briefly if we don't analyse every and each of these parameters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, it seems to me that you said that in this particular case, the fuse was set to --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On impact. To explode on impact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How then do you explain, Professor, that the shell broke the surface of the Markale market [Realtime transcript read in error "Madam Registrar"] and that the stabiliser embedded itself on to the ground? I think that you said that it was from 200 to 250 millimetres in depth. If the fuse was set to explode upon impact, how could this be possible?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The stabiliser has nothing to do with all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, you don't understand me. When the mine explodes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So a pause between question and answer, and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation Mr. President, I don't know if we see the same thing, but I see that the surface was -- we read something very strange. Maybe we should -- we see "Madam Registrar". What I see in my transcript is that "the surface of the Madam Registrar," "that the shell broke the surface of the Madam Registrar." It seems very painful and not very likely, Mr. President. So if we could please correct this for the transcript, first of all, for poor Mrs. Registrar and also for the transcript. I don't know if we have the same text, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you could have asked whether we could take it back at a certain line. That would have been enough instead of talking about things that are clear to everyone. Could you please resume, Ms. Pilipovic. The question was asked, Professor, it seems to me that you said in this particular case, the fuse was set -- and that it was to explode on the impact. I think if we restart from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you explain to us the following. How is it possible that the shell can embed itself into the ground? And we are talking about the ground covering the Markale market. So how is it possible that the stabiliser was able to get embedded into the ground at about 200 to 250 millimetres under the conditions that you have explained to us? You told us that the fuse was set to blast upon impact. Can you explain this to us, please?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that the shell went down and that it went right through from 200 to 250 millimetres. It is not the shell that was embedded, but the stabiliser. Secondly, upon the -- when a shell hits upon impact, the fuse activates itself, and the fuse transmits the detonation impulse onto the detonator. The detonator, therefore, transmits a further impulse onto the explosion. Then what happens is that detonation occurs, the projectile becomes larger, and just before exploding, its diameter enlarges from two to three times. And this all happens extremely briefly. It is a very short period of time. When the products of the detonation are stronger than the jacket, the resistance of the jacket, the jacket fragments, and the fragments of the jackets are blown away in the area surrounding the explosion. This happens all very quickly. The velocity of these fragments is enormous. And we talk about the stabiliser now. The same products of the detonation also act upon the stabiliser and they are contrary to the movement of the shell, which occurs just before the explosion. So depending on the velocity of the shell at the time of impact, the point of impact, the stabiliser can embed itself into a terrain or it can also be thrown away from the point of impact or it can also be found in the near vicinity of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. You have already explained this to us. I didn't want to interrupt you. Professor, you have told us that you were able to determine the angle of descent of the shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have found the range.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what is the range?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 10.5 to 65 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your statement that you gave on the 26th and on the 27th of February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not quite sure if we have a record of what exactly the questions and answers -- the last two questions and the last two answers are. Perhaps they can repeat it and the witness can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I believe the Professor said that it was from 55 and 65 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the -- yes. It is now clear. It was 55 to 65. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. I think, Mr. Stamp, in order to clarify the issue, when it was asked whether the Professor would have determined the angle of descent, he said, "I found a range." I understand it as not the exact angle but the range in which the angle should be located. Yes. And not the range of firing of something like that. That would be a totally different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know you have asked the witness and counsel to slow down, but may I ask the Court to remind the witness to begin answering at the end of the translation of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I asked several times not only for the speed of speech, but also to make a pause between answers and questions. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic, after you have taken a small pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you gave a statement to the members of the OTP on the 27th and 28th of February, 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In that same on page 2 of the said statement, the penultimate paragraph says the following, and I will just quote one line. You said: "We were able to determine the angle of the descent angle of the shell." Is that correct, "We were able to determine the angle of descent of the shell"?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be able to give me the page?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, 02 on the upper right-hand corner, the OTP attributed a number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We cannot speak at the same time since interpreters have only -- they have two ears, but they have only one mouth to pronounce the words. So you really have to slow down and to make pauses, otherwise, the Chamber will not be able to understand what the testimony is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the English version is 3502, that is the number of the page. And I am asking you to comment on the page 3501. And in B/C/S, we are talking about page 3493. It is the penultimate paragraph and it is the last word.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is not exactly what I said. Once again, I must say that we were able to determine from 55 to 65 degrees. That is in the official report that I signed, and I maintain what I said in that official report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, therefore, Professor, you are telling us that what is written in this statement that "We determined approximately the angle of descent of the shell," it is not correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is not precise, I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if you say, "approximately," that means it is within a certain range. If you really want to spend two or three minutes, you first started quoting without using the word "approximately," which is clearly in the statement. Then it perfectly coincides with the report. At least, until now, you say it is not precise. You say, "approximately." That is not precise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but the witness did say in his statement that he signed himself that it is approximately. I just really wanted to make sure what does he understand as "approximately."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, you said in your statement, and I am going to paraphrase, that a large number of people were injured in their lower extremities, lower limbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that because that is what I heard from people, and this is just a statement which is not contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't such a statement lead you to conclude that it doesn't really correspond to the fragments of a 120-millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, madam, it fully corresponds to the effect of a 120-millimetre shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a few more questions before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to ask you a few questions linked to the sound that the shell makes as it flies. At what distance, in your opinion, can you hear this sound when a shell is fired?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That depends on where you are and where the firing of the shell occurs. It depends whether between you and the source of the sound there are any obstacles. It depends on whether it is raining or not. It depends on whether it is snowing or not. All these factors have some effect on the intensity of the sound that people hear. So if you are on a flat area and there are no obstacles, the firing, the actual process when the shell leaves the mortar, can be heard at a distance of several kilometres. That is one possibility. If the mortar is in a valley or in a wood, in a forest, the intensity of the sound will be significantly reduced that you hear. If the person listening is in a town surrounded by high-rise buildings, they can muffle the sound of the firing. So there are many factors that have some effect on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, does the configuration of the ground affect the possibility of one hearing the firing of the shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also see the shell flying in the air?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me from which position?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From the position of an ordinary citizen.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. You see, when -- as a shell flies - this is the ballistic trajectory people - observing it from the side in some cases may be able to see the shell, depending on the height. The people who are standing in the direction of the flight of the shell cannot see it. A very important role in that respect is also played by the reflex of the background, the kind of sky, what the sky is like, whether it is cloudy, whether it is sunny. In some cases, it is possible to see it but that depends on the velocity of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is time for the break. With your permission, my colleague will have a few questions and we will complete our cross-examination before the two hours expire, so he will need another five minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. Are you not using your headphones or maybe you do not need them. Can you hear me? Thank you. Witness, I shall ask you a few questions quickly in French, and I should like to thank you in advance if you can to give me answers with a "yes" or "no." You stated that you were not authorised to take photographs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was not responsible for taking photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But what you said a moment ago, on page 4311, what was in English: "I was not authorised."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay, "authorised."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, at that point in time I was a civilian person. I was appointed by the Court without any support. I just asked for photographs to be taken, and the appropriate services fulfilled my wish, very simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But who was it that did not authorise you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant -- I did not have any support as president of the commission. I didn't have any support services which, in peacetime, any investigating commission would have. In Sarajevo, the conditions were emergency conditions. I drew attention to the need for photographs to be taken. I conveyed that to the judge. A photographer came, took photographs, and I thought I had nothing more to do with it. It was my duty to establish how the explosion had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, are you trying to tell me that things were done in haste?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which things, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The things connected to your inquiry.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My inquiry was over within 30 hours because I was asked by the judge, in order to have a clear picture of the whole case, that we should try to come to clear conclusions in the shortest possible time. My report and that of my colleagues is extremely precise and clear, and it was completed within a period of 30 hours, and there is no haste there. But it is a fact that the time factor was very important for the completion of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher and with your permission, I should like an exhibit which should be here, which is the stabiliser --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we open it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it may be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, while you are opening the parcel and to gain time, my next question will be -- you can take it out. Please do that. Are you holding in your hands what is called a stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, is it a 120-millimetre stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, have you already seen this object? Answer with a "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, does it correspond to the one that you examined?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is similar to it. That is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in your capacity as an expert who worked on this project, is it that stabiliser or not?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, no one on this whole world can tell you whether this is that stabiliser or not. The markings on this stabiliser are identical to the markings on those that are -- on the one that I examined, and that is all an engineer can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The object can be taken back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness you told us that the stabiliser was taken out from the marketplace before the beginning of your inquiry and that you, yourself, put it back later. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I didn't find the stabiliser there, that I saw on television that an attempt was made to take it out, and that I asked the stabiliser to be given to me, for me to try and place it back in the tunnel. That is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree with me, then, if I say to you that there is nothing to prove to you at the time that that stabiliser was the one that was allegedly found on the spot?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the report, a photograph is included of the spot immediately prior to the extraction of the stabiliser, and I got it from the police. It is part of the report. The photograph was small. If it is magnified, we can see whether the markings correspond. So I can only agree insofar that I was asked for the stabiliser, I was given the stabiliser, I put it back in the tunnel. And that is what it says in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Consequently, you could not know whether this stabiliser that you had in your hands was the one which allegedly hit the market or not?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With the exception of one point, and that is that this stabiliser in -- according to its length, could have fitted into the hole in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you arrived on the spot, what was the condition of the tunnel? Because the stabiliser had been moved, with the help of a knife, and consequently what was the condition in which you found that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me see. The entry part of the hole, that is where the fin of the stabiliser entered, was filled in with earth, whereas the bottom part of the tunnel into which the stabiliser had penetrated was relatively well preserved. So it was sufficient for me to use my finger to remove the surplus earth that had fallen into the hole so that, without any effort or without using any kind of force, to place the stabiliser into that tunnel. It is natural that 24 hours later -- after an incident of this kind, it is normal for the earth to enter that hole, but it is impossible not to consider the energy necessary for the stabiliser to penetrate. There must be a difference in the hardness of the ground. So that with any difficulty, I could remove the earth and place the stabiliser into the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, what you just told me is that the condition of the tunnel was not the same as it was 24 hours earlier?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it was like 24 hours previously. All I know is that the entrance into the tunnel was filled in with earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. So, we agree, Professor, that there was a manual operation that you engaged in yourself and that was necessary for you to do before replacing anything into that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before placing the stabiliser, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, on a technical level, and I would like you to answer me on that level, what would it mean if there was a simple 10-degree error in the replacing of such an object? I am speaking in general terms and not in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When there is such a delicate issue at stake, there is no general answer. The only criterion for determining the angle of descent was not the access of the tunnel. Another criterion was that a couple of metres from the place of detonation, there was a kiosk which had a roof. And if we were to draw a theoretical curve of the trajectory of the shell for the last 10 or 15 metres before impact, that minimum angle with which the shell would hit the point of impact without hitting the roof of that kiosk is just over 50 degrees. Therefore, in this case, with a very high degree of certainty, we can assert that the optimum angle of descent was between 55 and 65 degrees. Or rather as a referral angle, we used the angle of 60 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. In your inquiry, did you take the trouble to measure the distance from the point of impact in relation to the two facades of buildings on either side?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, can you confirm with a yes or no, is it correct to say that a simple error of a few decimetres regarding the localisation of the point of impact would have important consequences in relation to the distance in relation to this particular event, supposing that there was a firing of a weapon?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question is the following: Let us imagine that there was an error in measuring the point of impact itself, not the tunnel. Is it not true to say that such an error would have implications of all kinds on the technical analysis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Because I told you that the shell -- that had the shell hit the roof, then the angle of descent would be about 50 degrees. We took it that the angle is 60 degrees, and this is an enormous difference in the military use of shells. And if you noticed, no where in our report can you find the shell was fired from 5.382 metres, but it is said from the region between 4.900 -- about 5.800, about 6.400 metres, as I said today. Therefore, we took great care so that there would be absolutely no doubt that from the technical point of view, anybody could challenge the concept that I presented here. There is no error of that type because then I would not be a serious engineer in undertaking this study.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness Exhibit 68, D68, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question, since you did not make a pause. Yes, now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness Defence Exhibit 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While that being done, at page 71, line 6, I think it should be "4.900, about 5.000," not "5.800."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and not 5.800.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you Exhibit D68.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Before we proceed, may I just have a look at what the witness is being shown, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO, please, so we can follow questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this diagram of the buildings surrounding the Markale marketplace?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It looks like it. It looks like the marketplace of Markale, only the figures are not quite clear. The width of the street has not been indicated, the width of the pavement. For me to be able to answer with precision. But it looks like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, the diagram in the form of a star, the star in the middle of the diagram represents the point of impact. Can you read the distance in relation to the lowest building there.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says here on your diagram -- you are referring to this figure, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Six metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, does that agree with your own memories?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In my report, there is a very precise picture and the report is one that I signed, and it does not correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you yourself measure the point of impact?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document can be taken back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I shall like to go back to the question of fragments. You stated that you found two fragments?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As far as you know, where are they today?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Why should I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Because you are somebody in charge of weapons, because you found it, and you told us that you followed the trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...not whether you should know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that a chemical analysis of these elements would make it possible to provide interesting answers regarding the type of projectile in question?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A chemical and metallographical analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Quite so. So is your answer yes?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You stated a moment ago that you followed the trial in general terms. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The trial we are -- at which we are speaking.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Only occasionally, when I happened to be at home on Fridays and Saturdays, when reports on this trial were broadcast in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness before your testimony here, did you hear any other testimony?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you hear anything that had a direct or indirect connection to Markale?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you saw a televised feature with a French soldier removing this alleged stabiliser with a knife. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not a feature but just a clip of a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Is it not true to say, Witness, that when undertaking extraction of this kind, that is, by scratching with a knife, one will necessarily damage at least the upper part of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For your information, that is true. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when one damages the upper part of the tunnel and when the earth itself, due to the time that elapses, tends to fall in, would it not be correct to say that 24 hours after the event, the situation was relatively different when you returned than when allegedly that stabiliser was taken out of the ground?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Everything depends on the velocity of penetration. At high velocity, 24 hours doesn't mean anything. For low velocities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And 60 metres per second, is that a low velocity in relation to 310 or some other velocity?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Everything depends on the type of ground and what you are trying to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, Professor. I am asking you a technical question. A velocity of 60 metres per second, is it a low velocity compared to 310 metres, as you indicated to be a possible starting velocity?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I never said 310.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, never mind. Is the speed of 60 metres per second a low velocity?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The velocity of what? You can't ask me to say something if the velocity is not linked to the object, if you are talking about the velocity of the stabiliser or the velocity of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But that was your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, sir. I am telling you a shell can hit the target at velocities in the range of 200 metres per second, and the stabiliser, due to the effect of detonation products, penetrates the soil at a speed of 60 metres per second. So this is a major difference, technically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am speaking about the 60 metres per second. Are we talking of a relatively low velocity there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The question is not precise. For me as an expert witness to be able to give you a precise answer, you have to link it to the object. Was it a stabiliser or the shell that you are talking about? There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you can't give me an answer to that question, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You ask an impossible question. The witness -- because what you are doing, you are comparing the speed of firing with the speed of arrival. I could also ask someone whether 50 kilometres is a relatively low speed for a rocket. Of course, it very much depends on whether the rocket is transported in a truck or whether the rocket is fired or whether the rocket arrives somewhere or whether the rocket is used in a game where strong people have to push it. So you are making a comparison to the 310 metres per second, which was the firing speed. I think you would like to know from the witness - perhaps you could ask him - whether 60 metres per second, as the speed of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Penetration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not the speed of penetration. The speed with which a tail-fin or the last tail-fin would impact in the ground, would be a relatively high speed or a relatively slow speed, if you would compare that with the average speed with which tail-fins would impact on the ground after the mortar has detonated. I think if that is what you want to know, you should ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I thought we understood one another. We were speaking, Witness, of the speed of penetration.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So when you mentioned 60 metres per second, were you talking about the speed of penetration?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the stabiliser, of the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That velocity of penetration of 60 metres per second, in your opinion, is it a relatively low velocity or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Relatively high.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, I should like to move on to another line of questioning now. You indicated in your statement that in the town of Sarajevo, there were locations where weapons were being manufactured.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, is it true to say that you have relatively -- a relatively important position regarding armaments today?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that at the time -- I think your answer is yes, so I will withdraw the question. In your capacity as an engineer designing weapons, who has designed weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a clarification there? To the question, "Witness, is it true to say that you have a relatively important position regarding armaments today," could we just have the answer again please? The record indicates an answer of "no." My friend says that the answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be a translation mistake. We will check that. When you were asked whether you had a relatively important position regarding armaments today, was your answer "yes" or "no"? The answer was "no," Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdrew the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is that you distorted the answer of the witness and even --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely to clarify the question, Mr. President. That is why I said that I was withdrawing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said something before, but let's not spend time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know approximately how many other installations for the manufacture of weapons existed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean, "approximately"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: With precision or approximately, whichever you are able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can enumerate what I know, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, please do that.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the faculty of mechanical engineering, there was a small workshop with three lathes. In the Vaso Miskin Crni factory, a hall was used with perhaps 10 or so machines. In addition to that factory, I think there's another factory, and I can't remember its name exactly. It too had about 10 machines. In addition to the foundry at Alipasino Polje, there is another factory of reinforcement. I was never in that factory. I don't know how many machines it has, but probably 10 to 15. Let me remember. I know that in the brewery, there was also a small workshop for manufacturing weapons, and I think those are the ones I am aware of. Maybe later I will remember some more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am sure everyone will appreciate that. When you were talking about the brewery, could you tell us in which institute was it? Was it in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't, because I was never there. I never visited. Are you talking about the brewery or the workshop?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We come to my last set of questions. Are you aware of an operation code-named "Oxygen"?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you aware of an operation intending to import weapons to Sarajevo in oxygen bottles?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I read about that in the newspapers, but as an individual during the war, I was not aware of it. I knew -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But on the other hand, Witness, did you know how the BH Army procured its explosives for the manufacture of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you regarding the part I was in control of. As I was in the research and development department, this group belonged to the Main Staff of the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina. 40 per cent of all explosives that we obtained, I extracted from unexploded shells. I did so because in my unit, there were young men of 17, 18, and 20 years of age, and I was a professional. And every unexploded shell - and I have complete records about that - I would take off the fuse that didn't detonate and I prepared it for the extraction of explosives. This was in the period of June 1992 until June 1993, when my unit was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. You said that there were young men of 17 in your unit; is that true?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my unit, who worked on computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I consult my colleagues for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Just one point and my very last question: And are you aware of an operation called "Container"?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was not an important person in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And finally when you said 40 per cent of the ammunition, were you saying that 40 per cent of the shells targeting Sarajevo did not explode?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I am saying that 40 per cent of the explosive that my unit obtained, and it only produced hand grenades and rifle grenades, used ammunition from unexploded projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And the factory Zrak, did it manufacture hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't manufacture hand grenades. Hand grenades were partly manufactured at the mechanical engineering faculty. I think some in the Vaso Miskin factory also, but that is as much as I know. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My very last question. Is it correct that the BH army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...that you say it is your last question, it is your very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true that the BH army had mortar shells, mortars of 120 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Stamp, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just one or two questions arising from cross-examination, and there is one matter of formal clarification at the end of it which will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Defence showed you this exhibit, the tail-fin. And you said that the markings on that tail-fin that you have there now is identical to the one that you were presented to by the judge?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said also in cross-examination that something, and I am not sure what that thing is, was made at Krusik. What was it that you said was made at Krusik?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Krusik is a well-known factory for manufacturing mortars of 120 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is it you said was made at Krusik in respect to that particular shell or stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is the basic charge and the capsule which activates the basic charge, and this further on triggers the additional charge. This capsule activates the gunpowder, the gases go out through these holes and activates additional charge which then contributes to acceleration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your report that the shell -- or not in your report, in one of your statements, that the shell was either manufactured at Licki Osik in Croatia or at Pretis in Vogosca, but that it was most probably --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you explain quickly why, having regard to the colour of that stabiliser which you have in your hand or which you have there.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In our report, we noted that this stabiliser was not coloured. This is an unacceptable standard for a factory working under normal conditions. The Yugoslav standards were perfect in terms of surface protection, which provides for the stability for stocking such products. If colour is not put, this is a question of saving fuel, which happened when war was going on. This happened in Licki Osik and in the Pretis factories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. The Pretis factory is exactly where, do you know, in which municipality or area?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is in the Vogosca municipality, about 8 kilometres from the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1994 and 1993, can you say which party to the conflict was in control of that factory? And may I just ask it this way: When you respond, either say the army of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on this issue, lastly, to your knowledge, was the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994 in possession of that type of factory-manufactured shell without the paint?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't say that because I was no longer in the army then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You said that there was a factory in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From your report, is that -- can you remember the district or the area in Alipasino Polje where that factory was? Perhaps I could invite you to have a look at the page marked 3459 in the English version, which would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just try to find the page in the B/C/S version, in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3453.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having looked at the record of your statement, where in Alipasino Polje was this factory?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the casting plant. Casts were made there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, where? Where was this place?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Novo Sarajevo, across from the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you tell us the name of the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You gave the name of the street, wasn't it, or is that a different -- the old name of the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Dzemal Bijedic Street, the area across from the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that community was Livnica?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was called Alipasino Polje. The casting plant is the name of the factory Energoinvest, one of Energoinvest factory where casts were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the name of the factory? You said the casting plant is the name of the factory. That is the record that I have. What was the name of the factory in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the name of the factory or casting plant in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "Livnica" means casting plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I think the word "Livnica" means casting plant. And you said it was across from the --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Please forgive me. And you said it was across from the television station. How far was it from the television station?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: About 300, 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can you recall if it was to the south, north, east or west of the television station?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: North.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked questions about the scratching in the removal of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, may I ask you -- we are at a quarter to 2.00. You indicated that you would have one or two questions. Well, both parties seems to influence each other, a very last question, one or two questions. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not more than three to five minutes. I indicated that I would have one or two questions in respect of a formality at the end of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just -- because we have to plan and see whether we can finish or not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Judges will have questions as well and since the courtroom is used this afternoon for another case, I am afraid we cannot, unfortunately, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That we could not conclude today. And, therefore, I don't know whether the questions you still have are so linked to the questions that you asked already or whether they could be separated because otherwise -- they could be separated. Then I prefer to adjourn now because otherwise one of the other Chambers will think that it has become a habit to -- has become a habit to take their time. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I am just --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially since we have not -- we were not given the five minutes for our transcript business, I think we can do that on Monday in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I am just wondering, since we will have only a few questions left, whether it is necessary for your expert to stay with us or that he would like to return?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know what the future holds. The expert would like to be there also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am afraid for just half an hour next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am just informed that we would have another 10 minutes since the next case does not start at a quarter past 2.00. So let's try to see if we can finish today. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Quickly, Witness, if you could -- did the scratching that was done to the top part of this tunnel to remove this stabiliser fin, did it impact, in your opinion, to any significant degree on your measurement of the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In terms of measuring angles and erections, are you aware of the use of mils instead of degrees, which is occasionally done sometimes?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would you -- are you aware that an official UNPROFOR investigation -- may I rephrase. Are you aware that an official investigation by a team of experts was conducted by UNPROFOR about four or five days after your investigation?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I heard this on television. I was not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And on your report - and this is a question of formality, it doesn't really arise - your original report in your native language, and this is at page 385.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will see it is dated at the bottom, the 7th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you see at the bottom right corner where you have also signed it beside the date the 29th of September, 2001?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you signed it and dated it on the 29th of September, 2001 at the request of the investigators of the ICTY. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. That is the form that I just wanted to explain that date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before giving the opportunity to the other Judges to put questions, since you have this page in front of you, may I ask you one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is in the conclusions in photograph 7, the English translation, if we compare that with the original - I do understand that from your curriculum that you at least read English - the translation ends under 6 with "unclear." I do not see a similar indication under 6 in the original. It could be that the meaning was unclear to the interpreters or that the text was unclear, which is not -- the translation now reads: "The projectile came from the north, from the centre of the explosion." Is that what you intended?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that it came from the north, viewed in the direction of the flight. So it came from the north towards Markale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You could say that from the -- if you would make the explosion the place of impact, then it would have come from the north. So I think the unclarity was perhaps the language used. You have to clarify that. Thank you very much. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Were you able to determine what type of steel was used to make the shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You spoke about two fragments found in the place. Were those fragments from the shell or from the shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Those were the fragments that were found there that were produced after the explosion of the shell, and they are part of the body of the shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Are the fragments or the shrapnel indispensable, important, or useless, for determining the direction of the projectile?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They are not important for determining the direction or the possible location of launching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has, as I understand, one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] I would like you to clarify something for me in response to a question asked of you. It is about a brewery and a workshop producing ammunition. And you told us -- actually, I was not able to follow your answer. My question would be whether there was a brewery which had been transformed into a workshop manufacturing ammunition?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can I answer your question precisely? The brewery worked -- operated during the whole war, and as part of that brewery, there was a workshop for overhauling equipment. The machines for the mechanical process working of metal was also used for producing ammunition. So the factory, the brewery, was not transformed into an ammunition facility, but it was part of the factory that was a small workshop within it which was used for manufacturing ammunition. It is a question of two lathes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was located where?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was -- this factory was in the old part of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Near which building or in which neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was never in that workshop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, Professor Zecevic, I have a few questions for you. First question: Is there a maximum angle from which you could fire a mortar? Could you fire it at a 90-degree or is there any maximum angle?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Usually 85 degrees are used as a maximum for firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is almost vertical?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is more or less vertical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is: You explained to us that the power of the detonation would have a backwards effect to what follows, that is the stabiliser fin. Could it also influence the course of the stabiliser fin? Could it -- could the angle of impact being influenced by the, I would say, the backwards power caused by the detonation? Do you understand? I mean, would the stabiliser fin continue its course or could it be deflected in any way by this backwards power of the detonation?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The velocity of the shell at the time of impact is very important, which means that if the velocity of the shell is about 100 and then 60 or 70 metres per second, then the stabiliser will fall near the point of explosion. If the speed of the shell is 120, 130 metres per second, the stabilisers will fly backwards and will be 10 metres or so away. If the velocity of the shell is 200 or more metres per second, then the stabiliser will continue its trajectory and become lodged in the ground. The disruptions are short. This happens within the time frame of a microsecond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My last question, and it is just a clarification. Did I understand you well that the high velocity of the tail-fin, especially the first part of it, I would say the part with the small diameter, was such that the tunnel was relatively firm and that, therefore, it was not difficult to make a distinction between earth having fallen into that part of the tunnel and the relatively firm shape the tunnel itself?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your clarification. This then concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and having answered all the questions both of the parties and of the Bench. And I wish you a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. I think we have to deal with the paperwork next Monday. That would be preferable because otherwise this Chamber might build up a bad reputation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. And may I quickly, before the Court adjourns, just alert the Court and my friend that the Prosecution is seeking a clarification in respect to the Order of the Court not to include or receive in evidence the approximately 60 post-mortem reports? The clarification we seek is whether or not the Order includes three or four pages, which were attached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have been quite clear on that. I have said this report exists of two parts. First, we have the large series of post-mortem reports. If you would read the transcript, Mr. Stamp, it would be very clear to you. It is not the letter three four pages that I excluded, but just the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was clear to some of us. Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn until next Monday at a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
